Six conditions. One run. Controlled light.

blocks.en: Twenty‑four cultures under six defined light conditions at once. Green light induces protectant production and red halts it.

blocks.en: It took three design‑build‑test‑learn cycles. In Prototype 2 we measured 40 LEDs one by one (green varied by 26%, red by 22%) and matched them in fours, within 0.4–1.8%. Matching did not separate the intensity tiers, so the low, mid and high levels are set by PWM in code. Prototype 3 enclosed the array; overnight on a shaker a post snapped and the white holder leaked light between wells.

blocks.en: The first culture run, on 19 September 2026, grew in all six arms (3.1), but light leaked between wells, so it is not a light‑dose result. The fixes from that run are not yet re‑tested, and we have not yet run the intensity test the array was built for. Every reading here is in lux, which is weighted for human vision; it is not a biological light dose until it is converted to photon flux.

blocks.en: The LPA is a 24‑culture LED array we built to test how wavelength and light intensity affect our CcaS/CcaR optogenetic system in engineered Bacillus subtilis. We designed it around strain 168; it first ran on WB800, the protease‑deficient strain the project moved to in September (bioreactor, 2.2). Red and green LEDs give six light conditions, with four replicate cultures each.

blocks.en: The optogenetic system responds to light intensity and wavelength, so every well needs defined, even light. An Arduino sets the intensity by pulse‑width modulation, with one MOSFET per intensity tier, and a condition stays fixed for the whole run. The array, six columns of four with the MOSFET that drives each pair, is drawn in 4.2 Light Layout.

blocks.en: In Prototype 2 we worked on giving every well the same light. LEDs with very similar measured output were grouped into matched sets for each wavelength, and these sets became the low, mid and high columns.
blocks.text: In Prototype 2 we worked on giving every well the same light. LEDs with very similar measured output were grouped into matched sets for each wavelength, and these sets became the low, mid and high columns.

blocks.en: We drove each LED at 5 V and measured it on its own with a light meter, in a printed fixture that keeps the same distance and angle every time. Each LED got a tag with its row (A to D, downward) and column (1 to 5, across), so every LED can be traced back to its own reading. Then we rewired the array with the matched LEDs grouped into columns.

blocks.en: Matching cut the variation inside each group a lot. Before sorting, the green LEDs varied by 26% and the red by 22%; after matching, the four LEDs in a group differed by only about 0.4–1.7% for green and 1.5–1.8% for red. But matching did not give three distinct intensity levels. The low, mid and high groups were still too close, especially for green. The green high group was also a little less even than the other green groups, because it was made from the LEDs left over after the first two.

Before sorting, the green LEDs varied by 26% and the red by 22%; after matching, the four LEDs in a group differed by only about 0.4–1.7% for green and 1.5–1.8% for red. blocks.en: So we use matching to make each column even, and set the low, mid and high levels with the PWM duty cycle instead of by picking LEDs.

blocks.en: Each column of four is one light condition. A tier is a green and a red column on one MOSFET, so both share one duty cycle.
blocks.text: Each column of four is one light condition. A tier is a green and a red column on one MOSFET, so both share one duty cycle.

blocks.en: Why green and red?three reasons
Green turns production on. Green light activates the CcaS sensor, which switches on CcaR and, through it, the production genes.
blocks.text: Green turns production on. Green light activates the CcaS sensor, which switches on CcaR and, through it, the production genes.

blocks.en: Red turns it off. Red light switches CcaS back to its inactive form.
blocks.text: Red turns it off. Red light switches CcaS back to its inactive form.

blocks.en: So one array asks both questions. With both colors at three intensities, one run can show how strongly production follows the light and whether red stops it.
blocks.text: So one array asks both questions. With both colors at three intensities, one run can show how strongly production follows the light and whether red stops it.

blocks.en: The three MOSFETs and all 48 LED leads meet on one 160 × 100 mm perf board, screwed to the base plate’s four stands under the LED holder. Each tier’s eight minus leads are twisted together with its MOSFET’s drain lead and soldered across three holes on one side of the board: low on the left, medium on top, high on the right. All 24 plus leads meet the same way on the bottom side, wired to 5 V, and the three sources share a joint wired to GND. Jumpers on the gates go to Arduino pins D9, D10 and D11.

blocks.en: Safety. The LPA runs on 5 V. Unplug the Arduino and switch off the bench supply before changing any wiring, and do not look straight into the LEDs at full brightness (the guide’s “Before you start” page). The cultures are Bacillus subtilis, handled at BSL‑1 as set out on the team wiki’s Safety page.

blocks.en: The LPA is not a new idea. Lighting a plate of cultures from below, with control per well, is the Light Plate Apparatus design from the optogenetics literature1, and this LPA is named after it. We added the dual‑wavelength column layout, LEDs matched by measured output and an enclosure sized for our own tubes.
blocks.text: The LPA is not a new idea. Lighting a plate of cultures from below, with control per well, is the Light Plate Apparatus design from the optogenetics literature1, and this LPA is named after it. We added the dual‑wavelength column layout, LEDs matched by measured output and an enclosure sized for our own tubes.

blocks.en: The biology, the CcaS/CcaR green/red switch, also comes from the literature; Castillo‑Hair and colleagues characterized it in Bacillus subtilis2. This page reports light in lux and does not convert it to photon flux, so these tiers are not placed on that paper’s dose scale.

attrs.en: Summary
Judging criteria
LPA DBTL cycles
Cycle 1, stage by stage
The first LPA on a desk: a black printed LED holder with a few green and red LEDs lit, wired across to a breadboard and a microcontroller board.
Cycle 2, stage by stage
A round black printed fixture on a desk with one green LED lit at its centre, wired to the bench, the light meter's case behind it.
A row of loose LEDs laid along the edge of a desk, each pair of leads carrying an orange paper tag.
The black LED holder standing upright with green and red LEDs lit, tagged red and black leads running from it to a breadboard in front.
Cycle 3, stage by stage

The LPA assembled on a desk: a white 24-well tube holder seated in the top of a black printed housing, one lit tube standing in a corner well. Beside the housing, the Arduino sits on the desk on a clear base, with a USB-C cable and three jumper wires tagged P9, P10 and P11 running to the housing.

Close-up of the LPA on a lab shaker: the lower edge of the black housing with a screw, the grey bottom plate beneath it with white debris spread around a torn hole, a black rubber mat, and the shaker's blue front panel with a dial marked 60 and 80 and a strip of yellow tape by its knob.

A grey printed bottom plate with a cone-shaped base; fingers hold the snapped-off cylindrical post just above it, a screw through its top, with the perf board, three MOSFETs and dust on the plate behind.
The LPA running inside an incubator: twelve capped culture tubes glowing green and red in the white tube holder on the black housing, the Arduino and tagged wires beside it, on a shaker.
3D model of the LPA. Drag, or use the arrow keys, to turn it.
The LPA, assembled, at a three-quarter view: the black tube holder on the black housing, on its grey base plate, with the grey sliders at the sides.
Back to the starting view
Take it apart
The final LPA on a desk: a black printed tube holder with 24 round bores seated in the top of the black housing, the slider tab on its side.
The LPA's soldered board, three views

The green perf board on its four grey printed stands, the black LED holder resting above it: three upright MOSFETs in a row at its centre with black jumper housings on their legs, orange, purple and red jumper wires, and bundles of black and red LED leads under orange tape flags

The board's component side, drawn to scale. Three IRLZ44N MOSFETs, Q1 to Q3, stand in a row at the centre. Q1's gate goes to Arduino D9 and its drain to a three-hole joint on the left side, where the low tier's eight LED minus leads are soldered; Q2's gate goes to D10 and its drain to a joint on the top side for the medium tier; Q3's gate goes to D11 and its drain to a joint on the right side for the high tier. The three sources meet in a joint wired to GND, and all 24 LED plus leads meet in a joint on the bottom side wired to 5 V.

The solder side, seen from below and mirrored: solder on the nine MOSFET legs and five solder bridges, each across three holes: one on each side for a tier's LED minus leads and its MOSFET's drain, one for the 24 plus leads and 5 V, and one for the three sources and GND
